outcome: No result since 26 January 2024 changes the status of the conjecture; the only relevant events are (1) a 2025 paper by Jakimczuk that generalizes 'almost perfect' to an asymptotic condition σ(n)/n → β and is therefore a different, related problem, and (2) a February 2026 GitHub issue/PR in Google DeepMind's formal-conjectures repository that formalizes the open conjecture as an unproved Lean statement (`sorry`), not a proof.
summary: The classical conjecture — that every almost perfect number (σ(n) = 2n − 1) is a power of 2 — remains open, and I found no result in the window (26 Jan 2024 – 22 Sep 2026) that settles it, settles a case of it, or moves a bound on it. The current Wikipedia article on almost perfect numbers still states only the pre-2024 constraint (an odd almost perfect number greater than 1 would need at least six prime factors, from Kishore 1978/1981) and contains no discussion of any post-2024 progress. Two items surfaced in searching deserve explicit mention because they are close to the topic but do not count as progress on this bullet. First, Rafael Jakimczuk's 'A Note about Almost Perfect Numbers' (ResearchGate, uploaded 4 September 2025) proves results about a generalized, asymptotic notion — for a real β > 1, infinitely many n with ω(n) arbitrarily large and σ(n)/n arbitrarily close to β, with β = 2 termed 'almost perfect' in his paper. This changes the defining condition from the exact σ(n) = 2n − 1 used in the Wikipedia bullet to an approximate ratio condition, so under §3.1 it is a related problem (a variant sharing the same name), not a case of the stated problem; it does not remove any territory from the original question of whether an exact non-power-of-2 solution exists. Second, a GitHub issue (#2240, opened 10 February 2026) and associated pull request in Google DeepMind's 'formal-conjectures' repository formalize the exact classical conjecture as a Lean 4 statement — `∃ n, AlmostPerfect n ∧ ¬∃ k, n = 2^k` — but the proof body is `sorry`, i.e., unproved; the issue itself records a 'formalizability rating of 0/5' meaning it was judged trivial to state, not solved. This is bookkeeping/dataset infrastructure (a benchmark of open conjectures for formal-proof tooling), not mathematical progress, and involves no AI-generated proof content — it is a formal restatement of the already-known open question. No other 2024–2026 arXiv paper on near-perfect, superperfet, or within-perfect numbers touches the exact classical almost-perfect-number question either; each addresses a differently-defined class of numbers. I therefore record status `open` with `no_change_found` true.
competing_reading: One could argue the Jakimczuk paper is a genuine generalization whose β=2 case literally re-derives the classical almost-perfect condition in a limiting sense, so a skeptical reader might call it a weak form of 'partial' progress (e.g., existence of infinitely many n with σ(n)/n arbitrarily close to 2, though not equal). But the stated problem asks about exact equality σ(n) = 2n − 1, and 'arbitrarily close' does not restrict or settle any case of that exact equation — it is a different question about density/closeness rather than about the discrete equality, so I classify it as out of scope rather than partial.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or announcement giving either (a) an explicit non-power-of-2 integer n with σ(n) = 2n − 1, proved by hand or verified by computer algebra, which would resolve the conjecture in the negative-existence sense (refuted, i.e., such numbers do exist), or (b) a proof that no such n exists, which would confirm the conjectured characterization. Absent either, a completed (non-`sorry`) Lean proof of the formal-conjectures statement, checked and reviewed, would also count, at minimum as `claimed` pending expert digestion.
